Daily Devotional

December 22

4 And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:) 5 To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child. 6 And so it was, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered. - Luke 2:4-6 (KJV)

 The Christmas Story continues. Notice that Joseph went to pay his taxes, and that is a godly thing to do, as the bible says we are to owe nothing, but love, to any man (Romans 13:8). For a Christian to not pay his debts, including taxes, is the same thing as stealing, and certainly is not Christ like. Joseph was a descendant of David’s (Matthew 1:1-17), so he had to go to the city of David, called Bethlehem, to pay his taxes.

 To travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem, would have been about 69 miles by air, but on foot in probably would have been close to 80 miles or so. Can you imagine the hardship on Mary, being ready to deliver a child, to have to travel that far? And we think we have things tough now.

 When they got to Bethlehem, Mary went into labor. Think how hard it would be, to have been traveling for days, and then going into labor in a strange place – wow! It would have been much better for Mary to have been at home, and had a mid-wife help her with her delivery, but that was not what had been prophesized, so this was what had to happen for prophecy to be fulfilled. Praise God that all went well.

Devotional by Pastor Joe W. Green, www.Infinite-Faith.com

One of the VC funders to a healthcare company I worked for explained it to me very well. The issue starts with regulatory cost -- between the FDA and other government fiats (remember GW banning stem cell research to "save the babies" ...?) what used to cost about 500 Million (according to my funder) now costs in the billions. http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/cost-to-develop-new-pharmaceutical-drug-now-exceeds-2-5b/

Now, I'm not crying for the VCs because they are richer than Midas too, but it is really hard to make a business case to front a couple billion and then wait 10 years to start realizing returns. You and I have mortal lifetimes, and a lost decade is a lost decade, especially if a certain drug fails. Who doesn't have to worry about mortal lifespans and getting shit done in a timely manner? Governments.

What this does is force private investors and the marketplace out of contention, and shrinks the pool of private participants to only the wealthiest of the wealthy. Who CAN fritter away $2billion for 10 years and not care, is the government not State governments, mind you, only Federal/Sovereign. So now, instead of individuals paying, and researchers researching the stuff THEY WANT, researchers and academics have to go to a government research panel and beg the bureaucrats to give "grants" to make their project economically viable (remember it is the government wonks were the ones who drove up the price through regulation in the first place).

Some terrible consequences of this? The FDA shut down 23andMe to "protect the public" from having access to their own genetic data. A company was supplying a service, and people were happy buying it. The FDA infringed on all of our rights because they thought consumers were too stupid to understand that genetic markers for a condition didn't automatically equate to a diagnosis of said condition.

Another consequence is that although Google's project Calico, Craig Venter's Longevity, Inc., the SENS foundation, and others have decided that human aging is actually synonymous with the definition of "disease," the FDA still disagrees and blocks funding for said research. It takes the preposterously deep pockets of Google-esque organizations to stray from the FDA "program." So we are in a perverse space where the FDA is preventing health-extending, disease prevention research in favor of rubber-stamping big pharma cures for post-disease symptom treatment.

Having seen it up close and in person (and with the exception of a few luminaries and advanced centers of learning) the medical profession is depressingly mired in outdated thinking. It is the opposite of tech -- glacially-paced, fearful of innovation, mistrustful of technology, driven by crony physicians and their egos. Recently my dentist told me about how his alma mater is dead-set against teaching CNC-milled crowns and 3D modeling in their school curriculum -- because silver fillings still work. He has been trying for 7 years to get it on the curriculum, and the next review is something like 3 years from now, he said.

I don't like to throw around the over-used term "disruption" but if the tech industry can disrupt something, I can't think of a system more in need of it than healthcare in the US.
